rows.branch: All branches (the Tao Te Ching is read by philosophical readers and held as revealed scripture by the religious orders, Zhengyi and Quanzhen)
rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 60
rows.original: 非其神不傷人，聖人亦不傷人 (received Wang Bi and Heshang Gong text, from earlier project records); the Kanripo TLS edition reads 非其神不傷人也，聖人亦弗傷人也
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo); English: James Legge, The Tao Teh King, SBE 39 (1891), as recorded in earlier search ('neither does the ruling sage hurt them')
rows.says: Ruling a large state is like cooking small fish. When the world is ruled by the Tao, the spirits do not harm people, and neither does the sage. Since neither harms the other, virtue returns to both. It describes good rule; it is not worded as an order.
rows.bearing: A wider duty not to harm people (rule 7). Nothing limits who is protected, so it includes K1 and K0. The main Tier 1 basis, read with Tao Te Ching 49 and 27 and with Zhuangzi 17 and 22. Borderline: it describes the sage in the setting of ruling a state and does not name killing or private persons. Same basis as Article I row 7b.

The edition's 弗 and final 也 follow manuscript usage; the received reading 聖人亦不傷人 has the same sense (earlier search records; the received text itself is not local). Legge's English: VERIFIED (search), sacred-texts.com sbe39067.
rows.check: read directly and confirmed (edition variant recorded)

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 49 (received text 聖人無常心; the Kanripo TLS edition and the Mawangdui manuscript tradition read 恒)
rows.original: 聖人無常心，以百姓心為心。善者，吾善之；不善者，吾亦善之，德善 ... 聖人皆孩之 (Kanripo: 聖人無恒心，以百姓之心為心)
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo); English: James Legge (1891), as recorded in earlier search ('he deals with them all as his children')
rows.says: The sage has no fixed mind and takes the people's mind as his own. He is good to the good and good to the not-good as well, and so goodness is gained. He trusts the trustworthy and the untrustworthy alike. In Legge's reading he deals with them all as his children; some translators read 皆孩之 as 'makes them all childlike'.
rows.bearing: Sets the reach of the wider duty: it covers the not-good, so 'the wicked' are included (rule 7). It does not name killing, so on its own it is Implied for K1; read with ch. 60 it is part of the Clear teaching, borderline (as Article I row 7a).
rows.strength: Clear teaching, borderline (reach of the wider rule; read with ch. 60)
rows.verification: VERIFIED (direct, Kanripo KR5c0057, TLS base edition): KR5c0057_049.txt; seen: "善者吾善之，不善者吾亦善之，德善" and "聖人皆孩之". Legge's English: VERIFIED (search), ctext.org and the households check.
rows.check: read directly and confirmed

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 27
rows.original: 是以聖人常善救人，故無棄人 (Kanripo: 聖人恒善救人) ... 故善人者，不善人之師；不善人者，善人之資
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo); English: James Legge (1891), as recorded in earlier search
rows.says: The sage is always skilful at saving people, so he casts away no one; he does the same for things. The good person is the teacher of the not-good, and the not-good person is the good person's material (資).
rows.bearing: Universal care that excludes no one, the not-good included (reach, rule 7). It does not name harm or killing, so it supports the wider rule in ch. 60 rather than standing alone.
rows.strength: Implied alone; part of the Clear teaching, borderline, read with ch. 60 and 49

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 62
rows.original: 善人之寶，不善人之所保 ... 人之不善，何棄之有 ... 有罪以免邪 (Kanripo: 人之不善也，何棄之有；有罪以免耶)
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo); English: James Legge (1891), as recorded in earlier search ('Even men who are not good are not abandoned by it')
rows.says: The Tao is the treasure of the good and what protects the not-good. Even if people are not good, why should they be cast away? The ancients prized the Tao because by it those who seek find and those with guilt are spared.
rows.bearing: Reach of the wider rule (rule 7): the not-good are not cast off, and even the guilty are spared by the Tao. It describes the Tao, not a human duty, and does not name killing: Implied on its own. The line on the guilty concerns the Tao's grace, not human punishment, and does not limit K1.
rows.strength: Implied alone (reach of the wider rule)
rows.verification: VERIFIED (direct, Kanripo KR5c0057, TLS base edition): KR5c0057_062.txt; seen: "人之不善也，何棄之有" and "有罪以免耶". Legge's English: VERIFIED (search), sacred-texts.com sbe39069.
rows.check: read directly and corrected: the line 有罪以免, earlier unchecked, is now seen and described

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 81 (closing lines)
rows.original: 天之道，利而不害；聖人之道，為而不爭 (Kanripo: 故天之道、利而不害，聖人之道、為而弗爭)
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo); the English seen in search is an unidentified translation on sacred-texts.com 'Taoist Texts' (ttx02); Legge (1891) not seen
rows.says: The sage does not hoard; the more he does for others, the more he has. The Way of Heaven benefits and does not harm; the way of the sage is to act without contending.
rows.bearing: 'Does not harm' is said of Heaven's Way; the sage's own clause is 'does not contend'. So for a human duty it is Implied on its own. It supports ch. 60 by showing non-harm as the pattern of the Way. Legge is reported to read 利 as the 'sharpness' of Heaven's Way (unverified); either reading keeps 'does not harm'.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (direct, Kanripo KR5c0057, TLS base edition): KR5c0057_081.txt; seen: "故天之道、利而不害，聖人之道、為而弗爭". The English rendering remains VERIFIED (search), translator not identified (sacred-texts.com ttx02).
rows.check: read directly and corrected: the clause 利而不害 is in the text; the earlier record that Article I research saw ch. 81 without it is not borne out

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 63 (received Heshang Gong and Wang Bi texts; the Kanripo TLS edition agrees)
rows.original: 大小多少，報怨以德
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo); English: James Legge (1891), as recorded in earlier search ('recompense injury with kindness')
rows.says: Among the marks of acting by the Tao: act without acting, treat the great as small and the many as few, and recompense injury with kindness. Legge notes that the clauses describe the way of the Tao rather than give orders.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching against revenge, which covers K0's revenge clause (whoever answers injury with kindness does not kill for revenge). It does not name killing. A modern conjecture (unverified) moves the phrase to ch. 79; ch. 79 read directly in the same edition does not contain it, and ch. 63 does.

rows.check: read directly and confirmed

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 67
rows.original: 我有三寶，持而保之。一曰慈 ... 夫慈，以戰則勝，以守則固 (Kanripo: 我恒有三寶)
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo); English: James Legge (1891) ('gentleness'; others 'compassion'), as recorded in earlier search
rows.says: Laozi has three treasures: compassion, frugality, and not daring to put himself ahead of the world. Giving up compassion for boldness leads to death. Compassion wins in attack and holds firm in defence; Heaven protects by compassion.
rows.bearing: Compassion underlies non-harm, but the text does not name killing: Implied for K1 and K0. The line on compassion in war is context (rule 5).

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 42 (paragraph 3 in Legge)
rows.original: 強梁者不得其死，吾將以為教父
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo); English: James Legge (1891), as recorded in earlier search
rows.says: The violent and strong do not die their natural death; Laozi will make this the basis of his teaching. Legge reads it as self-exaltation leading to abasement.
rows.bearing: A warning about the fate of the violent, not a rule against killing: Implied.

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 4, Ren Jian Shi 人間世, section 1
rows.original: 命之曰菑人。菑人者，人必反菑之
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo), paraphrased by the project; Legge (1891) not seen
rows.says: Confucius warns Yan Hui that if he forces talk of benevolence and righteousness on a violent ruler, he shames the ruler and is called 'one who brings calamity on others'; whoever brings calamity on others will have calamity brought on him in turn.
rows.bearing: A prudential warning against harming others, set in advice about remonstrating with a tyrant; not a rule against killing: Implied.

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 74
rows.original: 若使民常畏死，而為奇者，吾得執而殺之，孰敢？常有司殺者殺。夫代司殺者殺，是謂代大匠斲 (received); Kanripo TLS: 若使民恒畏死，而為奇者，吾將得執而殺之，夫孰敢矣？若民恒且必畏死，則恒有司殺者殺
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo); English and note: James Legge (1891), as recorded in earlier search
rows.says: Threatening death is useless if people do not fear it. If they did, and wrongdoers could be seized and put to death, who would dare? But there is always One who presides over killing; whoever kills in his place is like someone hewing wood for the master carpenter, and seldom escapes cutting his own hands. Legge's note: the chapter shows that capital punishment fails and warns rulers against it.
rows.bearing: A ruler's punishment, so context only (rule 5). It presupposes judicial killing and warns against taking killing into one's own hands. By a fortiori argument it gives no warrant to a private person, but it does not say so: Implied for K1. It permits no private killing, so it does not contradict (rule 2).

rows.branch: All branches (Heshang Gong's commentary is transmitted within religious Taoism)
rows.reference: Heshang Gong commentary on Tao Te Ching 74, as summarised in Legge's note to ch. 74 (SBE 39)
rows.original: 司殺者 (read as 天, Heaven)
rows.translation: James Legge's English summary (1891)
rows.says: Heshang Gong identifies the One who presides over killing as Heaven, which dwells on high, rules all below and notes people's wrongdoing.
rows.bearing: The tradition's classical reading puts the right to take life with Heaven, so a human who kills on his own authority usurps it. It strengthens the reading of ch. 74 against private killing, but as Tier 2 it cannot decide a label (rule 1).

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 31
rows.original: 夫樂殺人者，則不可以得志於天下矣；殺人之眾，以哀悲泣之，戰勝以喪禮處之 (Kanripo: 以悲哀泣之; it opens 夫隹兵者 for the received 夫佳兵者)
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo); English: James Legge (1891), as recorded in earlier search
rows.says: Weapons are instruments of ill omen, not the instruments of the superior person, used only when there is no choice; calm restraint is best. To delight in victory is to delight in killing people, and whoever does so cannot get his will in the world. Whoever has killed multitudes should weep for them with grief, and victory is kept with the rites of mourning.
rows.bearing: War is context for K1 and K0 (rule 5). For K3 it limits all killing in war (only when unavoidable, never with delight, mourned) but does not single out people who are not fighting: Implied. Its condemnation of delight in killing bears on K0's 'hatred', but within war.

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 30, 68 and 69
rows.original: 以道佐人主者，不以兵強天下 ... 師之所處，荊棘生焉 ... 果而不得已 (30; Kanripo: 不以兵強於天下, 楚棘); 善戰者不怒 (68); 抗兵相加，哀者勝矣 (69; Kanripo: 則哀者勝矣)
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo), paraphrased by the project; Legge (1891) not seen
rows.says: Whoever helps a ruler by the Tao does not use arms to force the world; such deeds rebound; briars grow where armies have camped and bad years follow great armies; the good general gains his end and stops, does not boast, and acts only because he must (30). The good warrior is not warlike, the good fighter is not angry, the good victor does not engage (68). When opposing armies meet, the side that grieves wins (69).
rows.bearing: War, context only (rule 5); Implied for K3. Chapter 68 bears on K0's 'anger', but within war.

rows.tier: 1 (Zhuangzi, Miscellaneous Chapters; Su Shi doubted this chapter)
rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 28, Rang Wang 讓王, paragraph 2: King Tai Danfu of Bin
rows.original: 與人之兄居而殺其弟，與人之父居而殺其子，吾不忍也 ... 不以所用養害所養 ... 夫大王亶父，可謂能尊生矣
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo), paraphrased by the project; Legge (1891) not seen
rows.says: The Di attack Danfu's state of Bin and refuse skins, silk, dogs, horses, pearls and jade; they want the land. Danfu says he cannot bear to live with people's elder brothers while their younger brothers are killed, or with fathers while their sons are killed; one must not harm what is to be nourished with what nourishes it. He leaves, the people follow him, and the text says Danfu 'can be called one who honours life'.
rows.bearing: A ruler declining war, so context (rule 5). The text itself commends putting lives above land and goods, which bears on K0 ('for your own gain') and K3, but only by extension: Implied. Suicides elsewhere in the chapter fall under exclusion (d).
rows.strength: n/a (context); Implied for K0 and K3

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 24, Xu Wugui 徐无鬼, Xu Wugui and Marquis Wu of Wei
rows.original: 愛民，害民之始也；為義偃兵，造兵之本也 ... 无以戰勝人。夫殺人之士民，兼人之土地，以養吾私與吾神者，其戰不知孰善
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo); Legge (1891) for the first line as recorded in Article I research; the rest paraphrased by the project
rows.says: Xu Wugui tells the Marquis that 'loving the people' as a policy is the beginning of harming them, and 'ending war for righteousness' is the root of making war. Do not overcome others by cleverness, by scheming or by war. When one kills another state's officers and people and annexes its land to feed one's private ends, who knows which side is good, and where is the victory? Cultivate sincerity and the people will already have escaped death.
rows.bearing: K3 context: condemns wars of conquest and killing another state's people for private ends, but sets no rule protecting non-combatants within war: Implied. By extension it bears on K0's 'gain', within war. The 'love the people' line targets contrived benevolence (Article I, section I).
rows.strength: n/a (context); Implied for K3 and K0

rows.check: read directly and corrected: the 殺人之士民 line, earlier UNVERIFIED, is confirmed; 'for private ends' and 'do not overcome others by war' added

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 25, Ze Yang 則陽, King Ying of Wei and Marquis Mou of Tian (snail's horns parable)
rows.original: 魏瑩怒，將使人刺之 ... 君為萬乘之君也，而以匹夫從讎 ... 伏尸數萬
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo); Legge (1891) for the first line as recorded in earlier search ('The king was enraged, and intended to send a man to assassinate him'); the rest paraphrased
rows.says: King Ying of Wei, angry that the Marquis broke a treaty, means to have him assassinated. Xi Shou is ashamed: a ruler of ten thousand chariots should not take revenge like a common man; he asks for 200,000 troops to attack instead. Ji Zi calls Xi Shou a man of disorder; Hua Zi says those who argue for war and against it are all men of disorder. Dai Jinren's parable of two kingdoms on a snail's horns, whose war leaves tens of thousands dead, ends the king's anger.
rows.bearing: A ruler's order against another state, so context only (rule 5). The chapter approves neither the assassination nor the war. Revenge is spoken of as a common man's conduct by a speaker the text calls a man of disorder, not as a right: Implied (rule 4).

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 6, Da Zong Shi 大宗師, the True Man of old (古之真人)
rows.original: 以刑為體，以禮為翼，以知為時，以德為循。以刑為體者，綽乎其殺也
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo), paraphrased by the project; Legge (1891) not seen
rows.says: The True Man of old takes punishment as the body (of government), ritual as its wings, knowledge as timing and virtue as the path; taking punishment as the body means he is lenient (綽) in putting people to death.
rows.bearing: Judicial punishment, context only (rule 5). It accepts and tempers state killing and permits no private killing. Some editors are said to treat the passage as a later insertion (unverified).

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 4, Ren Jian Shi 人間世, section 1 (Yan Hui and the ruler of Wei)
rows.original: 輕用民死，死者以國量乎澤若蕉 ... 若殆往而刑耳 ... 且昔者桀殺關龍逢，紂殺王子比干 ... 堯攻叢枝、胥敖，禹攻有扈
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo), paraphrased by the project; Legge (1891) not seen
rows.says: Yan Hui tells Confucius that the young ruler of Wei uses his people's lives lightly, so that the dead fill the marshes like fallen grass, and he wants to go and correct him. Confucius warns that he will only get himself punished and die before the tyrant, as the tyrants Jie and Zhou killed the ministers Guan Longfeng and Bi Gan; he adds that even Yao and Yu, by waging war without end, left states empty and sought name and gain.
rows.bearing: Rulers' killings and wars, reported with disapproval: context only (rule 5); Implied.

rows.check: read directly and corrected: the 'uses his people's lives lightly' line is Yan Hui's, not Confucius's; the lines on Yao's and Yu's wars added

rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 11, Zai You 在宥; ch. 25, Ze Yang 則陽 (Bo Ju weeps over an executed man)
rows.original: 今世殊死者相枕也，桁楊者相推也，刑戮者相望也 (ch. 11); 曰莫為盜！莫為殺人！ ... 古之君人者，以得為在民，以失為在己 (ch. 25)
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo), paraphrased by the project; Legge (1891) not seen
rows.says: Ch. 11: today the executed lie pillowed on one another, the shackled jostle and the punished are everywhere in sight, while Confucians and Mohists strut among the fetters. Ch. 25: Bo Ju, a student of Lao Dan, finds an executed criminal in Qi, covers him with his robe and weeps: the world has a great calamity and you met it first; they say 'Do not steal! Do not kill!'; rulers set up what people suffer from and heap up what they fight over, then punish them; rulers of old took failures as their own fault.
rows.bearing: Criticism of state punishment: context only (rule 5); it limits rather than widens killing. The ban on killing is quoted as rulers' law and not disputed: Implied.

rows.check: read directly and corrected: was UNVERIFIED; the quoted bans, earlier added from memory, are confirmed

rows.reference: Tao Te Ching 5
rows.original: 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗；聖人不仁，以百姓為芻狗
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo); James Legge (1891) ('not benevolent'); some modern versions 'ruthless'
rows.says: Heaven and Earth, and the sage, are 'not benevolent' and treat creatures and people as straw dogs, ritual figures honoured in a sacrifice and thrown away after it.
rows.bearing: An image (rule 4), not permission to harm anyone. Its force depends on translation (translations.md). The same book says the sage harms no one (60), casts away no one (27) and is good to the not-good (49). Does not decide.

rows.check: read directly and confirmed

rows.tier: 2 (classical commentaries, used for reconciliation; not counted)
rows.branch: All branches (Heshang Gong transmitted within religious Taoism; Wang Bi the standard literati reading)
rows.reference: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, ch. 5; Heshang Gong, Laozi zhangju, ch. 5
rows.original: 天地任自然，無為無造 (Wang Bi); 不以仁恩，任自然也 (Heshang Gong, lead)
rows.translation: Classical Chinese, paraphrased by the project
rows.says: Wang Bi reads 不仁 as Heaven and Earth leaving things to their own course, neither acting nor creating; the benevolent must set up and teach, which makes things lose their true nature; earth does not grow grass for beasts, yet beasts eat grass. Heshang Gong also explains the line through 'what is so of itself' (自然).
rows.bearing: The tradition's own classical reading narrows ch. 5 to impartial non-interference, which removes any reading of it as licence to harm people. Reconciliation only (rule 1).

rows.original: 復讎者不折鏌干，雖有忮心者不怨飄瓦，是以天下平均。故无攻戰之亂，无殺戮之刑者，由此道也
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo), paraphrased by the project; Legge (1891) not seen
rows.says: Guan Yin tells Liezi that a drunk who falls from a cart is not killed because his spirit is whole, and that the sage, hidden in Heaven, cannot be harmed. One who takes revenge does not break the swords Moye and Ganjiang, and even a resentful man does not blame a tile the wind blows down; so the world stays even. That there are no disorders of attack and war, and no punishments of killing, comes from this Way.
rows.bearing: It presupposes blood revenge and uses it as an image (blame falls on agents with intent); it neither approves nor condemns revenge. Its own conclusion is a world without war or executions, so if anything it leans to support. Rule 4: Implied; does not decide K0 or K1.

rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo), paraphrased by the project; Legge (1891) not seen
rows.says: Robber Zhi leads 9,000 men across the world, raiding states, breaking into houses, driving off cattle and seizing women. When Confucius comes to reform him he is eating minced human liver; he threatens Confucius ('agree with me and live, oppose me and die') and routs him in debate. Zhi praises Shennong's age, when people had no mind to harm one another, as the height of virtue, and says the Yellow Emperor's war began the rule of the strong over the weak. Later Man Gou De lists the sage kings' killings ('Yao killed his eldest son ... the Duke of Zhou killed his elder brother') to mock Confucian order.
rows.bearing: The killings are reported, not approved; Zhi's own speech treats a world without harm as the height of virtue and condemns violent conquest. Rule 4: Implied; does not decide.

rows.original: 孰能以无為首，以生為脊，以死為尻 (ch. 6); 莊子則方箕踞鼓盆而歌 ... 雖南面王樂，不能過也 (ch. 18)
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo), paraphrased by the project; Legge (1891) not seen
rows.says: Ch. 6: four friends agree that whoever sees life and death as one body is their friend, and meet sickness and death calmly. Ch. 18: Zhuangzi drums on a pot and sings after his wife's death, saying her life and death are like the seasons; a skull in a dream says death has no ruler above or subject below and that even a king's joy cannot surpass it.

rows.original: 劍士夾門而客三千餘人，日夜相擊於前，死傷者歲百餘人 ... 臣之劍，十步殺一人 ... 劍士皆服斃其處也
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo), paraphrased by the project; Legge (1891) not seen
rows.says: King Wen of Zhao keeps more than 3,000 swordsmen who fight before him day and night; more than a hundred are killed or wounded each year, and the state declines. Zhuangzi, posing as a swordsman ('my sword kills one man every ten paces'), persuades him that the commoner's sword-fight is no better than a cockfight and useless to the state. The king stays in his palace three months, and the swordsmen all die in their quarters (服斃, commonly read as taking their own lives).
rows.bearing: A ruler's lethal sport, treated as ruinous and ended: Implied support rather than counter. Zhuangzi's boast is a ruse within the story. The swordsmen's deaths fall under exclusion (d).

rows.translation: Classical Chinese, paraphrased by the project
rows.says: In the land of Zhemu east of Yue, when the eldest son is born he is cut up and eaten, which is said to be good for his younger brothers; when the grandfather dies the grandmother is abandoned. rows.reference: Zhuangzi ch. 14, Tian Yun 天運, Lao Dan's answer to Zigong on the rule of the Three August Ones and Five Emperors
rows.original: 堯之治天下，使民心親，民有為其親殺其殺，而民不非也 ... 禹之治天下，使民心變，人有心而兵有順，殺盜非殺人，自為種而天下耳，是以天下大駭，儒墨皆起 ... 名曰治之，而亂莫甚焉
rows.translation: Classical Chinese read directly (Kanripo), paraphrased by the project; Legge (1891) not seen
rows.says: Lao Dan tells Zigong that the rule of the Three August Ones and Five Emperors, called order, was the worst disorder. Under the Yellow Emperor people did not weep for dead parents and no one blamed them; under Yao people 'killed [or reduced] for their kin' (為其親殺其殺) and no one blamed them; under Shun children were pushed to grow fast and early deaths began; under Yu hearts changed, arms were thought proper, and 'killing a robber is not killing a man' was held, which alarmed the world and gave rise to the Confucians and Mohists. (Kanripo punctuates 殺盜非殺，人自為種; the usual reading is 殺盜非殺人.)
rows.bearing: (a) 殺其殺 is a disputed word: 'kill those who killed one's kin' (revenge left unblamed) or 'reduce mourning by degree'. Either way it is one stage of a decline the teacher calls the worst disorder, so it is not approval (rule 4). (b) 'Killing a robber is not killing a man' is a status exception that Lao Dan presents as a mark of decline: if anything the text rejects it. Neither decides. Guo Xiang's and Cheng Xuanying's readings of 殺 were not checked.

K1.label: Not contradicted; taught (borderline), through a wider rule
K1.reason:
Rule 7. The deciding texts are all Tier 1, accepted by every branch, and VERIFIED (direct) in Kanripo:
- Tao Te Ching 60: the sage does not harm people (received 聖人亦不傷人; Kanripo 聖人亦弗傷人也). This is a wider duty not to harm, and it includes not killing.
- Tao Te Ching 49 (good to the not-good) and 27 (casts away no one): these set its reach to everyone, 'the wicked' included.
- Zhuangzi 17 (the Great Man's conduct does not go out to harm people) and Zhuangzi 22 (the sage harms no being; only one who harms nothing can meet people): these teach the same non-harm as the ideal person's conduct, with no reference to ruling.

It is borderline for three reasons:
1. Every one of these texts describes the ideal person rather than laying down a rule. The project reads the sage as everyone's model (Article I, note 6).
2. The Tao Te Ching basis (ch. 60) is set in ruling a state. The texts that free non-harm from office are Outer Chapters, which corpus.md weights below the Inner Chapters.
3. No counted text names deliberate killing by a private person as forbidden. The one 'Do not kill!' in the counted texts (Zhuangzi 25) is quoted as rulers' law within a critique of punishment. Newborns are covered only through 'people' (rule 9). No classical commentary was checked.

Rules 2 and 3 are not met. No counted text permits, commands or approves a killing by a private person, a household head or a crowd, or makes a killing blameless because of who the victim is. The hard texts are reports or images (rule 4):
- Zhuangzi 14: under Yao, people 'killed for their kin' unblamed; under Yu, 'killing a robber is not killing a man'. Lao Dan presents both as stages of a decline he calls the worst disorder.
- Zhuangzi 28: 'whoever killed the Master would not be held guilty'. This is the disciples' description of a lawless age, not a ruling.
- Zhuangzi 19: revenge used as an image, ending in a world without war or executions.
- Zhuangzi 25: revenge called a common man's act by a speaker the text calls a man of disorder.
- Zhuangzi 10 and 29: robbers and the killing of a ruler, as satire.
- Tao Te Ching 5: the straw dogs, read by Wang Bi as non-interference (VERIFIED (search)).

Rulers' punishment (Tao Te Ching 74; Zhuangzi 6 以刑為體; Zhuangzi 14, 生殺 as an instrument of correction) and war (Tao Te Ching 31; Zhuangzi 6, the sage's use of arms) are context only (rule 5).

For consistency: Numbers 35:27 and Abū Dāwūd 4361 are counted texts that themselves declare a private killing free of guilt or retaliation. No Taoist counted text does this. The nearest Taoist passages are reports set in a narrative of decline or danger, and the teacher in the text never says the act was right.

Rule 6 does not apply. The disputed word 殺其殺 (Zhuangzi 14) sits in a report the teacher condemns, so neither reading makes it approval.

Reported beside the label (Tier 2, not deciding):
- Ganying Pian: Explicit against killing people for their wealth (VERIFIED (search)).
- Lingbao Ten Precepts: the first precept is 'do not kill' (VERIFIED (search); status undecided).
- Liezi: the report of a foreign people who eat their firstborn (VERIFIED (search); flagged). It is a report under rule 4 and does not decide.

If the project lead holds that the ideal person's non-harm does not bind private persons, the label falls to Silent (rule 8), not Contradicted.

K0.label: Not contradicted; taught (borderline), through a wider rule, with Clear teaching against revenge
K0.reason:
K0 is narrower than K1, so the same wider rule covers it (Tao Te Ching 60 with 49 and 27; Zhuangzi 17 and 22; all VERIFIED (direct)).

In addition:
- Revenge: Tao Te Ching 63, 報怨以德 ('recompense injury with kindness'), is Clear teaching against revenge (VERIFIED (direct)). It does not name killing. Both the received text and the Kanripo edition place it in ch. 63, and ch. 79 in the same edition does not contain it.
- Gain: Zhuangzi 17's 'does not act for gain' is part of the same Clear teaching passage.

Implied support, all read directly:
- Tao Te Ching 79: a settled enmity leaves resentment, and the sage makes no demands.
- Tao Te Ching 46: no fault is greater than the wish to get.
- Tao Te Ching 68: the good fighter is not angry (set in war).
- Zhuangzi 23: sons killing fathers and ministers killing rulers for gain is the root of disorder.
- Zhuangzi 20: an infant is saved instead of jade.
- Zhuangzi 24 and 28: killing for private ends or for gain in war is condemned (context).

Borderline on the same grounds as K1, though the revenge clause has its own Clear teaching.

No counted text approves killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge:
- Zhuangzi 19 presupposes revenge as an image.
- Zhuangzi 25 treats revenge as beneath a ruler, and its speaker is called a man of disorder.
- Zhuangzi 14's 殺其殺 is a disputed word inside a condemned decline.

Reported beside the label (Tier 2, not deciding):
- Ganying Pian: killing people for their wealth (Explicit; VERIFIED (search)).
- Initial Perfection Ten Precepts, precept 2: do not secretly plot harm to others for one's own benefit (VERIFIED (search), content only; Quanzhen).

K3.label: Not contradicted; silent in counted texts (Implied only)
K3.reason:
Rule 8 with rule 1. Every counted war text was read directly:
- Tao Te Ching 30: do not use arms to force the world; stop when the end is gained; act only because one must.
- Tao Te Ching 31: weapons only when unavoidable; delight in killing is condemned; the slain are mourned.
- Tao Te Ching 68: the good fighter is not angry.
- Tao Te Ching 69: the side that grieves wins.
- Zhuangzi 6 (Inner Chapters): the sage may destroy a state without losing its people's hearts.
- Zhuangzi 24: killing another state's officers and people for one's private ends is condemned.
- Zhuangzi 25: war is mocked.
- Zhuangzi 28: Danfu will not have his people's sons killed for land, and Wu Guang says killing the people is not humane.

These restrain all killing in war, but none singles out children, the old, civilians or those who have surrendered: Implied. No counted text approves killing people who are not fighting. Only the Ganying Pian (Tier 2, VERIFIED (search)) condemns slaying those who have surrendered or submitted.

Parity caveat, unchanged: if the project lets a general non-harm rule reach conduct in war, as the secular humanism check did, then Tao Te Ching 60 read with 31 would give 'taught (wider rule), borderline'. Zhuangzi 6's acceptance of the sage's wars does not block that, because it approves no killing of non-combatants. The project lead should decide this once, for every tradition.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: Rule 7 is applied to K1 and K0 but withheld from K3, and the proposal itself admits that the secular humanism check did the opposite. In this run's research summaries (scratchpad a2/show_HU.txt, show_CO.txt, show_BU.txt, show_JA.txt), secular humanism and Confucianism give K3 'taught (wider rule), borderline', and Buddhism and Jainism give 'taught (wider rule)'; Hinduism, Sikhism and the Bahá'í Faith give Silent. Nothing in the rules stops rule 7 reaching K3: rule 5 makes war context for K1 and K0, but K3 is itself the war wording. Taoism's case is at least as strong as humanism's. (a) The wider rule reaches all people and all beings: Tao Te Ching 60 (聖人亦弗傷人也) and Zhuangzi 22 (聖人處物不傷物), both read directly. (b) Unlike the humanist declarations, the counted texts also speak about war, and they limit killing in it to what cannot be avoided: Tao Te Ching 31 (不得已而用之; delight in killing condemned; the slain mourned) and 30 (果而已 ... 果而不得已), both read directly. Deliberately killing people who are not fighting falls outside the texts' own necessity limit, just as the humanism check said self-defence is aimed only at attackers. (c) Zhuangzi 6's sage destroys a state 'without losing its people's hearts' (亡國而不失人心, read directly), which points towards sparing them, not against it. (d) No counted text approves killing people who are not fighting. Keeping Silent as the default for Taoism while humanism and Confucianism default to taught gives like texts different labels.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7 (a wider duty counts if it reaches everyone the wording protects); rule 8 (Silent only when no counted text either way); METHOD.md section 3, 'Wider rules'; the consistency requirement in the task.
objections.proposed: Not contradicted; taught (borderline), through a wider rule (Tao Te Ching 60 and Zhuangzi 22, read with Tao Te Ching 30 and 31). This is provisional on one project-wide ruling. If the project lead rules that a general non-harm rule does not reach conduct in war, the label becomes Silent, and the same ruling must then move humanism, Confucianism, Buddhism and Jainism too. Borderline because no counted text names non-combatants, Tao Te Ching 31 accepts 'killing multitudes' (殺人之眾) in unavoidable war without telling combatants and others apart, and the only explicit line (Ganying Pian 誅降戮服) is Tier 2.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Borderline ground 3 ('no counted text names deliberate killing by a private person as forbidden') and the Tao Te Ching 74 row ('it does not say so') understate what ch. 74 says. Read directly: 夫代司殺者殺，是謂代大匠斲也。夫代大匠斲者，則希有不傷其手矣. The subject is anyone who kills in place of the one who presides over killing. A private killer is the plainest case, and no a fortiori step is needed. This holds whether the presiding one is Heaven (Heshang Gong, as reported by Legge) or an official executioner. Zhuangzi 25 (Bo Ju, read directly) also treats 莫為殺人 ('Do not kill!') as the standing norm for ordinary people. The Taoist speaker blames rulers for driving people to break it, but never questions the ban itself. Both texts stay Implied: ch. 74 is a prudential image in a chapter about ruling, and Bo Ju only quotes the ban. So the label does not move, but the stated ground is wrong.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7 and METHOD.md section 3 strength ratings; the no cherry-picking rule (support must be stated accurately as well as counter-evidence).
objections.proposed: Keep the label. Reword ground 3: 'No counted text states a rule against private killing as such. Tao Te Ching 74 warns anyone who kills in place of the presiding killer that the act rebounds on him, and Zhuangzi 25 treats "Do not kill!" as the people's norm. Both are Implied.' Change the ch. 74 row's bearing to match.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Three counted passages that report killings (all read directly) are missing from the counter rows. K1 expressly binds crowds, so the first one matters most. (1) Zhuangzi 28: Liezi refuses Zi Yang's grain, and then 其卒，民果作難而殺子陽 ('in the end the people did rise up and kill Zi Yang'). This is a crowd killing, reported as proof that Liezi was prudent, and the text never says it was right. (2) Zhuangzi 23 (Gengsang Chu): 為不善乎顯明之中者，人得而誅之 ('whoever does wrong in the open, men will punish or put to death'). It presupposes human punishment and authorises no private killing. (3) Zhuangzi 29: Zhi cites 子路欲殺衛君而事不成 (Zilu's failed attempt to kill the ruler of Wei) as a failure of Confucius' teaching, so the act is reported and blamed.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 4 (reporting is not approving); rule 5 (courts context; crowds not excluded); the hard rule to search for counter-evidence and show it.
objections.proposed: Add the three rows as counter rows, all Implied under rule 4 (the Zhuangzi 23 row under rule 5 as context). No label changes.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The Tier 1 text in corpus.md is the received Wang Bi and Heshang Gong Tao Te Ching, but the rows marked 'VERIFIED (direct)' read the TLS base edition, which uses manuscript readings. The received wording rests only on search records. Decision 6 requires every counted citation to be read directly before admission. Ch. 74 is where this matters most. The edition's 若民恒且必畏死，則恒有司殺者殺 reads naturally as naming a standing office of executioner, while the received 常有司殺者殺 is the line Heshang Gong reads as Heaven. So the row's 'the sense is unchanged' is too strong, and corpus.md asks for variants that change the meaning to be recorded. This does not change K1, because under either reading a private killer kills 'in place of' the presiding one.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 1 (only verified counted texts decide); METHOD.md section 9, decision 6; corpus.md section 7 (record manuscript variants where they change the meaning).
objections.proposed: Record these rows as 'VERIFIED (direct) in the TLS edition; received wording VERIFIED (search)'. Read the received Wang Bi text of chs 49, 60, 63 and 74 directly before admission. Note the ch. 74 variant as one that changes who the presiding killer is, while leaving K1 untouched.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The Liezi is set aside mainly because it is Tier 2. But corpus.md records that it was honoured as a 'true scripture' (zhenjing) in 742, and the Zhuangzi received the parallel title Nanhua zhenjing in the same year (general knowledge, not checked here). Decision 4 has not been applied to the Liezi for the religious branches. If it were counted for them, the Zhemu passage would need testing under rule 3, and the result turns on its unverified closing line. Read as 未足為異 ('not to be thought strange'), it is a report or a relativist remark (rule 4). Read as 未足為非 ('not to be thought wrong', the Bowuzhi variant), it comes close to rule 2's 'declares wholly blameless'. Compare Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 ('not anger but reason'), which was counted against Stoicism.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 1 and branch rule; rule 3; rule 4; METHOD.md section 9, decision 4; consistency with the Seneca hard case.
objections.proposed: Keep the label. Say in the reasoning that even if the Liezi were counted for the religious branches, the passage is a report under rule 4 only if the Liezi reads 異. Verify the closing line before admission, and ask the project lead to apply decision 4 to the Liezi.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The Silent fallback is incomplete. Its trigger is that the ideal person's non-harm does not bind private persons. The Lingbao Ten Precepts text (VERIFIED (search); first precept 不殺，當念眾生) is a scripture (經) presented as spoken by the Celestial Worthy. If decision 4 treats it as primary for the Lingbao and Zhengyi ordination branches, the fallback is not plain Silent. It becomes 'Silent in texts every branch accepts; taught (Explicit, wider rule) in the religious branches'. The same applies to K0.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Here is the strongest case that K1 is too gentle. I reject it, but the reasoning should face it. The Inner Chapters, the layer corpus.md weights most, give only Implied support (Zhuangzi 4, 菑人). They also accept the sage's war and his lenient executions (Zhuangzi 6, 亡國而不失人心 and 綽乎其殺). The Hundun row glosses Zhuangzi 7's 勝物而不傷 as 'deal with things without harm', but in context (the mirror that 'responds but does not store') it is often read as the perfect man not being harmed by things. So it must not be cited as Inner Chapter non-harm. The Clear teaching therefore rests on one ruling-state chapter (Tao Te Ching 60) and the Outer Chapters (17, 22). It survives only through Article I note 6 and decision D3, and that is why it stays borderline, not taught.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7; METHOD.md section 3 ('Clear teaching must not be stretched'); corpus.md section 7 (Inner Chapters carry most weight).
objections.proposed: Keep 'taught (borderline)'. Add to the borderline grounds that the Inner Chapters give only Implied support and themselves accept the sage's war and executions. Note the alternative reading of 勝物而不傷 in the Hundun row.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The Zhuangzi 14 row reads 怨恩取與諫教生殺，八者，正之器也 as government on the strength of usage alone. The text names the user of these instruments only as 'one who follows the great changes without obstruction'. If Guo Xiang or Cheng Xuanying read this as the perfected person's personal use of 'killing' as a tool of correction, rule 5's last sentence (a killing whose judicial or private character is disputed) could bring rule 6 into play. No such dispute has been found, so the context reading stands for now.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 5 (last sentence); rule 6; corpus.md section 7 (Guo Xiang and Cheng Xuanying named for reconciliation).
objections.proposed: Keep as context. List the Guo Xiang and Cheng Xuanying check as required before admission.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: The revenge clause rests on Tao Te Ching 63's 報怨以德. The received text and the TLS edition (read directly, with ch. 79 confirmed not to contain the line) support placing it in ch. 63. But the Guodian slips' version of ch. 63 is, as I recall from memory and without checking, shorter and may lack 大小多少，報怨以德. corpus.md requires Guodian variants that change the meaning to be recorded. The received text is Tier 1, so this would not move the label. K0's anger and hatred clauses rest only on the wider rule: Tao Te Ching 68 and 31 are war texts (context). The reasoning should say so plainly.
objections.proposed: Keep the label. Check and record the Guodian reading of ch. 63 before admission. State that the anger and hatred clauses are taught only through the wider rule.

K1.label: Not contradicted; taught (borderline), through a wider rule
K1.reason: Rule 7. Counted Tier 1 texts accepted by every branch, read directly in the TLS edition: Tao Te Ching 60 (the sage does not harm people), with 49, 27 and 62 setting its reach to the not-good; Zhuangzi 17 (the Great Man's conduct does not go out to harm people) and Zhuangzi 22 (the sage harms no being), which state non-harm as the ideal person's conduct outside office. Implied support that narrows the gap: Tao Te Ching 74 (whoever kills in place of the presiding killer seldom escapes cutting his own hands) and Zhuangzi 25 (Bo Ju treats 'Do not kill!' as the people's norm). Rules 2 and 3 are not met. No counted text permits, commands or approves a private, household or crowd killing, or declares one blameless because of who the victim is. Zhuangzi 14 (殺其殺; 殺盜非殺人) sits in a decline Lao Dan calls the worst disorder. Zhuangzi 28 (殺夫子者无罪) is the disciples' description of an outlaw's plight. Zhuangzi 28 (the crowd that kills Zi Yang), 23, 29, 19, 25, 10 and Tao Te Ching 5 are reports or images (rule 4). Tao Te Ching 74, Zhuangzi 6 and 14 (生殺) are court context (rule 5). Borderline because: every deciding text describes an ideal person rather than stating a rule; the Tao Te Ching basis is set in ruling a state; the Inner Chapters give only Implied support and themselves accept the sage's war and lenient executions; no counted text states a rule against private killing as such; newborns are covered only through 'people' (rule 9); and the received text and the classical commentaries have not been read directly. The Liezi Zhemu passage (Tier 2, flagged) is a report if its closing line reads 未足為異. That line must be verified. If the ideal person's non-harm is held not to bind private persons, the label falls to Silent in texts every branch accepts, and to 'taught' in the religious branches if the Lingbao precept scripture is counted for them.

K0.label: Not contradicted; taught (borderline), through a wider rule, with Clear teaching against revenge
K0.reason: K0 is narrower than K1, so the same wider rule covers it (Tao Te Ching 60 with 49 and 27; Zhuangzi 17 and 22). Revenge: Tao Te Ching 63, 報怨以德, is Clear teaching, read directly in ch. 63, and ch. 79 in the same edition does not contain it. The Guodian reading still needs checking. Gain: Zhuangzi 17's 動不為利 sits in the same Clear teaching passage as its non-harm line. Implied support: Tao Te Ching 79 and 46; Zhuangzi 23 (killing fathers and rulers for gain as the root of disorder); Zhuangzi 20 (the infant saved instead of jade); Zhuangzi 24 and 28 (killing for private ends or gain in war condemned, as context). Anger and hatred are taught only through the wider rule, since Tao Te Ching 68 and 31 are war texts. No counted text approves killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge. Zhuangzi 19 uses revenge as an image, Zhuangzi 25's speaker is called a man of disorder, and Zhuangzi 14's 殺其殺 sits inside a condemned decline. The Ganying Pian and the Initial Perfection precept 2 (Tier 2) agree but are reported beside the label. Borderline on the same grounds as K1, apart from the revenge clause.

K3.label: Not contradicted; taught (borderline), through a wider rule; provisional on a project-wide ruling
K3.reason: Rule 7 applied to K3 as the secular humanism and Confucianism checks applied it. The wider rule (Tao Te Ching 60; Zhuangzi 22, the sage harms no being) reaches every person. The counted war texts limit killing in war to what cannot be avoided (Tao Te Ching 31, 不得已而用之; 30, 果而不得已), condemn delight in killing and require mourning. Deliberately killing people who are not fighting falls outside that necessity limit. Zhuangzi 6's sage destroys a state without losing its people's hearts, and Zhuangzi 24 and 28 (Wu Guang: 殺民，非仁也) condemn killing people in war for private ends or gain. No counted text approves killing children, the old, civilians or those who have surrendered, so rules 2, 3 and 6 are not met. Borderline because no counted text names non-combatants, Tao Te Ching 31 accepts the 'killing of multitudes' in unavoidable war without telling combatants and others apart, and the one explicit line on those who surrender (Ganying Pian 誅降戮服) is Tier 2. If the project lead rules that a general non-harm rule does not reach conduct in war, the label is Silent (Implied only), and that ruling must be applied to every tradition whose K3 rests on a general rule.

challenge.consistency_notes: Hard cases. Numbers 35:26 to 27 and Abū Dāwūd 4361 are counted texts in which the law, or the Prophet, declares a private killing free of bloodguilt or retaliation. The nearest Taoist text, Zhuangzi 28's 殺夫子者无罪, is the disciples' description of an outlaw's plight, and the teacher never rules on it. So rule 4 applies, not rule 2, and the distinction holds. Phinehas: no counted Taoist text rewards a zealot. Zhuangzi 29 reports Zilu's attempt to kill the ruler of Wei as a failure. Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2: the author approves newborn drowning in his own voice. No counted Taoist text does this. The Liezi Zhemu report (Tier 2, flagged) is the only near case, and it stays a report only if its closing line reads 未足為異, not 未足為非, so that line must be verified. The Liezi's 742 zhenjing status, parallel to the Zhuangzi's, also means decision 4 should be applied to it. Mahāparinirvāṇa icchantika (a status exception): Zhuangzi 14's 殺盜非殺人 is a status exception, but Lao Dan presents it as a mark of decline, so the text rejects rather than approves it. Yasna 31.18 and 33.2 (harming the follower of the Lie): Tao Te Ching 49 and 62 require goodness to the not-good, and no counted text commends harming the wicked. Atharvaveda rites and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12: no counted Taoist text describes a rite or act to kill a person; religious ritual texts outside the corpus were not checked. Crowds: the Zi Yang killing (Zhuangzi 28) should be shown as a rule 4 report, as crowd texts are shown for other traditions. Wider rules: K1 and K0 use the route Article I used for Taoism (note 6, rows 7a and 7b), and the borderline rating is kept for the same reasons as in the households annex (TA-1). K3: the run is split. Secular humanism, Confucianism, Buddhism and Jainism apply a general rule to war, while Hinduism, Sikhism and the Bahá'í Faith do not. Taoism's proposed Silent sided with the second group although its case (a universal non-harm rule plus war texts limiting killing to the unavoidable) matches the first. I have aligned it with humanism and Confucianism as 'taught (borderline), provisional', and the project lead should settle the split once for all thirteen. Verification: the Tao Te Ching rows were read directly in the TLS edition, not in the received text that corpus.md names. This gap should be stated plainly so that Taoism is not shown as more strongly verified than it is, and it should be closed before admission.
